strengths: The paper studies an important and timely failure mode of text-to-image diffusion models: spatial relation generation and object composition. Framing this through mechanistic interpretability is original for CV/T2I and potentially useful beyond benchmark chasing.

The controlled synthetic setup is well matched to the mechanistic questions. The authors separate colors, shapes, object bindings, and spatial relations, and evaluate multiple DiT sizes and text-encoder variants rather than relying on a single trained model.

The evidence for different RTE-DiT and T5-DiT mechanisms is interesting: attention synopsis identifies candidate heads, head-specific ablations affect relation/shape accuracy, and T5 token-vector interventions causally shift generated layouts while mostly preserving object identity.

The appendix provides substantial methodological detail: dataset construction, model sizes, training settings, sampling, deterministic evaluation, prompt-template robustness, and variance partitioning. This improves interpretability of the reported results.
weaknesses: The external validity is limited. The main claims are drawn from a very simple synthetic world with two objects, three shapes, two colors, gray backgrounds, fixed image resolution, and templated prompts. The paper sometimes extrapolates toward real-world T2I bottlenecks and text-encoder design more strongly than the evidence supports.

The causal circuit evidence is suggestive but not fully conclusive. Ablating the RTE relation head reduces relation accuracy substantially but does not isolate the full computation, and the object-head ablation has a modest effect. More complete path patching, activation patching across layers/timesteps, or necessity/sufficiency tests for the proposed two-stage circuit would strengthen the mechanistic claim.

The T5 robustness result is intriguing but confounded by training-distribution/template effects. Adding filler words or changing template structure may simply move prompts out of the narrow synthetic training distribution; the paper does not show whether training with augmented templates removes the failure or whether the proposed embedding mechanism remains causal under such augmentation.

The evaluation lacks uncertainty reporting in key tables. Table 2 averages many samples, but confidence intervals, seed-to-seed variance, and training-run variance are mostly absent, making it hard to judge reliability of differences such as RTE versus T5 robustness or effects of weight decay.

The attention synopsis method is useful, but it depends on generated-object masks and category aggregation, which can introduce circularity or obscure alternative information routes. The paper would benefit from stronger validation that the synopsis does not miss distributed or redundant circuits.

There are some inconsistencies and clarity issues. The main text emphasizes eight spatial relations, while the dataset appendix also describes occlusion/front-behind relations; it is not fully clear how these are used or excluded in training/evaluation. Several claims and figures are hard to parse without more precise definitions of interventions, ablation masks, and exact sample counts.

Reproducibility is incomplete for a mechanistic paper. The authors state code and datasets will be released upon acceptance, but current reproducibility relies on prose descriptions. Given the complexity of instrumentation, ablations, and vector arithmetic, unavailable code is a meaningful limitation.

strengths: The paper studies an important problem: why text-to-image diffusion models struggle with spatial relations, and it frames the question through mechanistic interpretability rather than only benchmark improvement.

The controlled synthetic setup is useful for isolating relation, object identity, and binding factors, and the comparison between random token embeddings, random embeddings with position, and T5 is a sensible axis of investigation.
The proposed attention synopsis is a practical analysis tool for reducing a very large set of cross-attention maps into interpretable layer/head summaries.

The RTE-DiT findings are supported by multiple forms of evidence: head localization, head ablation, QK/VO inspection, and an intervention suggesting a relation head can tag locations used by a later object head.
The manuscript includes substantial appendix detail on dataset generation, model configuration, evaluation logic, and additional attention visualizations.
weaknesses: The central claims are much broader than the evidence supports. All main experiments are on a small synthetic dataset with two colored geometric shapes and models trained from scratch; this does not justify strong implications about real-world T2I systems or text encoders being the bottleneck in practical spatial-relation failures.

The performance claims are overstated. The paper repeatedly describes near-perfect task learning, but Table 2 reports best loose spatial accuracy around 0.84 and strict spatial accuracy around 0.76 for the main RTE-DiT-B setting; T5 variants also collapse under minor prompt changes. This weakens the premise that the circuit explains a reliably solved task.

There are concerning inconsistencies in experimental reporting. The main text mentions 96 evaluation prompts, while Table 2 reports 264 prompts with 50 samples each; the main task description says eight spatial relations, while the appendix dataset generation also includes in-front/behind occlusion relations. These inconsistencies make it difficult to know exactly what was trained and evaluated.

The evaluation metric may inflate success. The main spatial relation score uses a loose criterion that accepts diagonal configurations for cardinal relations, while strict results are notably lower. Since the paper is about spatial precision, relying on the loose metric should be better justified and analyzed.

The causal evidence for the proposed circuits is incomplete. Head ablations show performance drops, but the relation-head ablation baseline in the text reports 67% accuracy, differing from the main table values; object-head ablation has a relatively small drop. The injection/vector-arithmetic interventions are mostly qualitative and do not establish that the described circuit is necessary and sufficient across prompts, seeds, and model sizes.

The T5 mechanism is less convincingly established than the RTE mechanism. The conclusion that relation information is decoded from shape tokens rests on token masking, representation visualization, variance partitioning, and qualitative vector arithmetic, but lacks enough quantitative causal patching or controls to rule out other explanations such as distribution shift, EOS dependence, or prompt-template memorization.

Robustness/generalization is narrow. Adding a filler token is an informative perturbation, but the paper does not evaluate broader paraphrases, unseen object combinations, more objects, different layouts, real images, or pretrained T2I models. This limits the usefulness of the conclusions for CVPR audiences interested in general computer vision systems.

Reproducibility is currently limited: the paper says code, configurations, and datasets will be released only upon acceptance. Given the many implementation-sensitive claims about attention recording, ablation, evaluation, and training dynamics, lack of released artifacts is a material weakness.

Presentation quality is uneven, with grammar issues, some imprecise terminology, and occasional speculative analogies. These are less important than the methodological concerns, but they make the technical claims harder to assess confidently.

strengths: The paper asks a timely and interesting mechanistic question: how DiT-style text-to-image models implement spatial relations, rather than only measuring that they fail or succeed. The controlled synthetic setup is well matched to circuit analysis and makes the claims more inspectable than they would be in open-domain T2I models.

The central comparison between random token embeddings with positional encodings and frozen T5 embeddings is original and informative. Showing that similar in-domain accuracy can arise from different internal mechanisms is a meaningful contribution for both interpretability and compositional generation.

The evidence for the RTE circuit is fairly strong: attention synopsis localizes candidate heads, the QK analysis connects relation tokens to spatial gradients, and targeted ablations/manipulations support a two-stage relation-head/object-head mechanism.

The T5 analysis is also valuable: token masking, variance partitioning, and embedding-vector interventions collectively support the claim that relation information is fused into contextual object-token embeddings rather than read directly from relation words.

The appendix provides substantial implementation detail on dataset generation, model variants, sampling, evaluation, attention logging, and variance partitioning, which improves reproducibility if the promised code is released.
weaknesses: The empirical setting is narrow: 128x128 synthetic scenes with two simple colored shapes, fixed prompt templates, and a small vocabulary. This is appropriate for mechanistic study, but the discussion sometimes extrapolates too strongly to real-world text-to-image failures and text-encoder bottlenecks without experiments on pretrained/open-domain T2I systems.

Several quantitative claims are overstated or internally uneven. The abstract says all models learn the task to near-perfect accuracy, but Table 2 reports spatial relation accuracy around 0.81-0.86 for the best main settings, much lower strict accuracy in some variants, and poor performance for RTE without positional encoding and nano models. The main text also mentions 96 prompts while Table 2 reports 264 prompts, which should be reconciled.

The T5 circuit evidence is less complete than the RTE circuit evidence. The masking result appears to rely on a specific prompt/setting in the main figure, and the embedding arithmetic intervention is mainly qualitative; broader quantitative intervention results across relations, shapes, seeds, and prompt templates would make the causal claim stronger.

The robustness/generalization conclusion is interesting but limited. The perturbations are small template changes such as inserting 'the', and the training distribution already contains template/paraphrase structure. It remains unclear whether the observed T5 fragility reflects the proposed mechanism generally, dataset/template artifacts, tokenization effects, or insufficient coverage during training.

The evaluation pipeline is deterministic and transparent, but it depends on threshold-based segmentation and loose spatial criteria. More analysis of evaluator failure modes, confidence intervals across training runs/seeds, and stricter reporting in the main text would make the performance evidence more convincing.

Reproducibility is not yet complete because code and data are only promised upon acceptance. Given the mechanistic claims depend on custom instrumentation, attention aggregation, and interventions, public artifacts or more precise release-ready details are important.

Presentation has noticeable clarity issues and typos, including 'casual manipulation' instead of 'causal manipulation', occasional grammar problems, and some small figures/heatmaps that are hard to read. These are mostly fixable, but they do make parts of the evidence harder to verify.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and under-explored problem: how text-to-image diffusion transformers implement multi-object spatial relations, rather than only measuring whether they succeed. The controlled setup is well matched to mechanistic analysis, with explicit variation over text encoders, model scale, prompt templates, and spatial relations.

The main empirical finding is interesting and plausible: DiTs trained with random token embeddings appear to learn a more modular two-stage circuit, where relation-oriented cross-attention heads create spatial gradients and later object heads bind object identity to those tagged regions, while T5/CLIP-conditioned models rely more on contextual object-token embeddings that already mix relation and object information.

The evidence goes beyond passive attention visualization. The paper includes targeted head ablations, causal manipulations/injections, token masking, weight-space screening, variance partitioning of contextual embeddings, and robustness tests under prompt perturbations. This triangulation makes the interpretability claims more convincing than attention-map inspection alone.

The work is potentially useful for both interpretability and T2I model design. The attention synopsis and weight-space head screening procedures could be reused to study sparse relation-sensitive heads in other DiT models, and the comparison between disentangled versus contextualized text conditioning offers a concrete hypothesis for why spatial relations remain brittle.

The appendices provide substantial implementation and methodological detail, including dataset construction, model sizes, training/sampling setup, evaluation metrics, variance partitioning, and head-screening formulas.
weaknesses: The central experiments are conducted on a very simplified synthetic task: two objects, three shapes, two colors, eight relations, gray background, and highly regular prompt/image structure. This is appropriate for circuit discovery, but it limits the strength of conclusions about real-world T2I spatial reasoning, where object appearance, occlusion, scale, compositional clutter, and linguistic variation are much richer.

The paper sometimes overstates performance and generality. The main table reports in-domain all-correct performance around 0.75 for DiT-B with RTE/T5 and substantially lower performance for smaller models, so phrases such as near-perfect accuracy are not fully supported unless referring only to selected submetrics. Similarly, the pretrained PixArt-Sigma analysis finds nontrivial object/relation accuracy for only 8 of 30 object pairs, making transfer to real pretrained systems suggestive rather than strong.

The mechanistic claims are compelling but not fully closed. Ablating the RTE relation head reduces relation accuracy substantially, and ablating the object head affects shape accuracy, but residual performance remains; for T5/CLIP the circuit evidence is more indirect and depends on supervised variance-factor extraction from known prompt factors. The paper would benefit from clearer separation between necessary components, sufficient components, and useful correlates.

The robustness conclusions are based on a narrow set of synthetic prompt perturbations. The observed T5 brittleness to filler-token insertion, locative inversion, and color synonyms is interesting, but the training distribution is also narrow; it is hard to tell how much reflects the proposed circuit mechanism versus ordinary out-of-distribution prompt-format sensitivity from training on templated captions.

The evaluation relies on hand-engineered segmentation/classification with OpenCV and task-specific binary metrics. This is reasonable for the simple dataset, but the paper should more clearly report failure modes, confidence intervals or variance over seeds, and whether metric errors occur, especially because several claims hinge on differences of tens of percentage points across ablations or perturbations.

Reproducibility is weakened by the code availability section being incomplete: it states that code, configurations, and datasets are publicly available but provides no visible URL in the manuscript. Given the custom training, evaluation, attention instrumentation, and intervention code, this omission is material.

Presentation is uneven. Some figures and captions carry a large burden of evidence, but many quantitative details are relegated to appendix figures without enough numerical reporting in the main text. There are also grammar and terminology issues, such as inconsistent use of RTE with/without positional encoding and occasional typos, that make the argument harder to follow.

strengths: The paper studies an important and timely failure mode of text-to-image diffusion models: spatial relations between multiple objects. The focus on mechanisms rather than only benchmark performance is a worthwhile direction for computer vision and generative modeling.

The controlled synthetic setup is well designed for mechanistic analysis: simple shapes/colors, eight spatial relations, multiple model scales, and multiple text encoders make it possible to isolate factors that would be hard to study in full natural-image models.

The comparison between random token embeddings, T5, and CLIP is interesting. The observation that similar in-domain accuracy can arise from different circuits, with different robustness to prompt perturbations, is potentially useful.

The paper includes several forms of evidence beyond attention visualization, including targeted head ablations, causal embedding/vector manipulations, variance partitioning, prompt perturbation tests, and some transfer analysis to PixArt-Sigma.
The appendix is extensive and contains many additional experiments, including model-scale comparisons, prompt-template evaluations, CLIP-based analysis, and pretrained-model probing.
weaknesses: The main scientific claims are much broader than the evidence supports. Most core conclusions are derived from a highly synthetic two-object shape/color dataset and DiTs trained from scratch. The connection to real text-to-image systems remains weak, especially because the PixArt-Sigma experiment reports very low spatial accuracy and only limited nontrivial behavior for 8 of 30 object pairs.

The claimed task mastery is overstated. The abstract says models learn to near-perfect accuracy, but the main table reports spatial-relation accuracies around 0.81-0.86 for the best in-distribution settings, stringent spatial accuracy often around 0.61-0.76, and much worse performance for smaller models, RTE without position, and perturbed T5 prompts.

The evaluation pipeline relies on hand-engineered OpenCV segmentation/classification for very simple rendered shapes. This is acceptable for the toy setup, but it limits the conclusions and is not validated enough to support broader claims about spatial relation generation in vision models.

The causal evidence is suggestive but not fully convincing. Head ablation effects are sometimes partial rather than decisive, object-head ablation only reduces shape accuracy from 90% to 76%, and several causal/vector-arithmetic results are presented qualitatively or without enough statistical uncertainty, controls, or failure analysis.

The T5 robustness result is interesting but partly reflects a mismatch between training and test prompt distributions in a small synthetic language space. The paper should be more careful about distinguishing circuit brittleness from insufficient template diversity during training.

The method relies heavily on attention-based interpretations and designed factor decompositions. Although the authors add ablations, the paper does not sufficiently rule out alternative explanations such as distributed redundancy, effects of positional encodings, training-template shortcuts, or analysis choices in the variance partitioning procedure.

Reproducibility is incomplete in the manuscript: the code/dataset availability section says all code and datasets are available at, but the actual URL is missing. Important training details, compute cost, random seed variability, and exact implementation choices are also not always easy to recover from the text.

The paper is presentation-heavy and sometimes imprecise. There are grammar issues, terminology mistakes such as “RTE w/pos” being defined as without positional encoding, overclaimed biological analogies, and no clear limitations section. These issues do not by themselves warrant rejection, but they compound the concern that the claims are ahead of the evidence.

The contribution to CVPR is borderline from an empirical vision standpoint: the mechanistic story is interesting, but the practical usefulness for improving real T2I spatial reasoning is not demonstrated, and the strongest results remain confined to a toy domain.

strengths: The paper addresses an important and timely problem: why text-to-image DiT models fail or succeed at spatial relation generation, moving beyond benchmark scores toward mechanistic explanations.

The controlled synthetic setup is well chosen for circuit analysis: two objects, explicit attributes, eight spatial relations, multiple text encoders, several DiT scales, and deterministic evaluation make the core phenomena measurable.

The evidence for the RTE-DiT circuit is relatively strong. The authors combine attention synopsis, QK/VO analysis, targeted head ablation, and a causal manipulation showing that the relation-head output can drive the downstream object head.

The comparison between random token embeddings, T5, and additional CLIP experiments is original and useful. The finding that similar in-domain accuracy can arise from quite different circuits is a meaningful contribution.

The robustness analysis is a notable strength: small prompt perturbations strongly affect T5-DiT but not RTE-DiT, and the proposed explanation via perturbations of the shape-token relation factor is plausible and supported by additional analysis.

The appendix contains substantial implementation detail on dataset generation, evaluation, model architecture, variance partitioning, and head screening, which improves interpretability of the results.
weaknesses: The main conclusions are established primarily in a very simplified synthetic world with three shapes, two colors, simple backgrounds, and discrete relations. This is appropriate for mechanistic study, but limits how strongly the paper can claim implications for real-world T2I failures.

The pretrained-model evidence is much thinner than the synthetic evidence. PixArt-Sigma has weak spatial performance in the authors' evaluation, and the analysis is demonstrated on a small subset of object pairs and essentially one high-performing prompt, so transfer to real deployed models remains suggestive rather than convincing.

Some causal claims are stronger than the evidence warrants. The ablations and embedding edits support functional relevance of identified heads/features, but they do not fully rule out distributed backup mechanisms or show necessity/sufficiency across the full prompt and seed distribution.

The T5 factorization analysis assumes a linear additive decomposition of contextual embeddings into relation/object/color factors. The paper uses it effectively as a probe, but the interpretation as a clean internal representation may be over-strong without additional controls or comparisons to alternative decompositions.

The evaluation pipeline is tailored to simple rendered images using thresholding and contour heuristics. This is acceptable for the synthetic task, but it also means that reported accuracy is not directly comparable to standard T2I spatial-reasoning benchmarks.

There are presentation and reproducibility issues: the code availability section states that code and data are public but the link appears missing, and parts of the manuscript contain grammatical errors, formatting glitches, and occasional overstatements such as suggesting all models reach near-perfect accuracy despite scale and robustness failures.
